description: Earth, Wind & Fire's breakthrough No. 1 hit from That's the Way of the World (1975), written by Maurice White, Larry Dunn and Philip Bailey. A starlit walk in Colorado became a Grammy-winning anthem of self-belief.

pops.text: Written by Maurice White, Larry Dunn and Philip Bailey — three of the band's core creative engine in one songwriting credit.
Maurice White got the idea on a walk under star-filled skies in the mountains around Caribou Ranch, Colorado, a famous '70s recording retreat.
The song comes from That's the Way of the World — which began life as the soundtrack to a film of the same name starring Harvey Keitel, with the band playing the group he produces.
The movie flopped. The album did the opposite: No. 1 on the pop chart for three weeks, and Columbia Records' biggest seller of 1975.
Chart double: 'Shining Star' spent two weeks at No. 1 R&B and also hit No. 1 on the pop chart in 1975 — Earth, Wind & Fire's mainstream breakthrough.
It won the Grammy for Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals — the band's first Grammy Award.
The band recorded the soundtrack album without even seeing the finished film — Verdine White later admitted he didn't think it had been completed yet.
Hall of Fame twice over: the album That's the Way of the World was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2004, and 'Shining Star' itself followed in 2008.
Pop culture immortality: this is the song Elaine dances to in Seinfeld's 'The Little Kicks' (1996) — George's verdict: 'a full-body dry heave set to music.'
Earth, Wind & Fire were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2000 — and yes, they performed 'Shining Star' at the ceremony.

title: Shining Star

description: The opening track and lead single from All 'n All (1977), written by Maurice White, Verdine White and Sonny Burke. A funk hit built on the kundalini idea of energy rising up the spine — seven weeks at No. 1 on the soul chart.

pops.text: First sound you hear on All 'n All: 'Serpentine Fire' is the album's opening track, released as a single on October 15, 1977, ahead of the album.
Written by brothers Maurice and Verdine White with Reginald 'Sonny' Burke, produced by Maurice for Kalimba Productions and arranged by Tom Tom 84.
The title is philosophy in disguise: Maurice White described it as an abstract lyric about kundalini energy — the 'serpent fire' said to rise from the base of the spine.
Parent album All 'n All grew out of Maurice White's month-long trip to Argentina and Brazil — he later said Brazil saved him and re-energized the band.
Soul-chart marathon: 'Serpentine Fire' spent seven weeks at No. 1 on Billboard's Hot Soul Songs chart.
Billboard went further and named it the R&B single of the year.
It crossed over too, reaching No. 13 on the Billboard Hot 100.
Flip the 45 over: the B-side was simply an instrumental version of 'Serpentine Fire' itself.
Columbia issued a music video for the song in October 1977 — years before MTV existed to play it.
All 'n All hit No. 1 R&B and No. 3 on the Billboard 200, was certified triple platinum, and won a Grammy for Best R&B Vocal Performance by a Duo, Group or Chorus.

title: Serpentine Fire

description: Eddie Money's debut single, written with guitarist Jimmy Lyon and released in December 1977 from his self-titled debut album. A working-class rock plea that climbed to No. 11 and launched a run of eleven Top 40 hits.

pops.text: First single, first hit: 'Baby Hold On' was released in December 1977 as the debut single from Eddie Money's self-titled debut album.
Written by Money with his guitarist Jimmy Lyon — whose simple, catchy guitar line opens the song.
Chart report: No. 11 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 4 in Canada and No. 19 in Australia on the Kent Music Report.
Spot the flip: 'Whatever will be, will be / the future is ours to see' rewrites Doris Day's 'Que Sera, Sera,' which insisted the future's NOT ours to see.
Before rock: Edward Joseph Mahoney was a New York City police trainee, following his father, grandfather and brother — he left in 1968 to pursue music.
The name is a joke on himself: he shortened Mahoney to Money and kept it sarcastic, because at the time he was always broke.
Promoter Bill Graham took him on as manager and mentor and helped land the Columbia Records deal behind this album.
He first heard it on the radio driving his 1962 Studebaker in San Francisco — KFRC AM played it, and he raced to a payphone to call his mother.
Her review? It was Wednesday — her mahjong night — and she told him not to call on Wednesdays. Showbiz, meet Mom.
The debut album went double platinum, and the song kept living: it later turned up in Rock Band 3 and Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories.

title: Baby Hold On

description: Eddie Money's 1986 comeback smash from Can't Hold Back, built around the Ronettes' 'Be My Baby' — sung by Ronnie Spector herself. It hit No. 4, topped the rock chart and earned Money a Grammy nomination.

pops.text: Career rescue: released August 16, 1986 as the lead single from Can't Hold Back, after a low point in Money's career — producer Richie Zito brought him the song.
The chorus interpolates the Ronettes' 1963 hit 'Be My Baby' — which is why Ellie Greenwich, Jeff Barry and Phil Spector share writing credit with Mike Leeson and Peter Vale.
First choice wasn't Ronnie: Money initially invited Martha Davis of the Motels to sing the 'Be My Baby' lines — she told him to go get the real thing.
So he phoned Ronnie Spector at home in northern California and pitched it as a tribute to her. The lyric 'just like Ronnie sang' is what won her over.
That's really her: Spector reprises her own iconic line, 'be my little baby,' uncredited on the record.
His biggest U.S. hit: No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 on November 15, 1986, and No. 1 on the Album Rock Tracks chart.
It earned Money a Grammy nomination for Best Male Rock Vocal Performance at the 1987 awards — he lost to Robert Palmer's 'Addicted to Love.'
The black-and-white video, directed by Nick Morris, was shot at the Lawlor Events Center in Reno: Money alone on an empty stage with a ladder, a folding chair and his alto sax.
Spector is kept in makeup rooms and hallways for most of the video — her face isn't fully revealed until about three-quarters of the way through.
Double comeback: Can't Hold Back went platinum for Money, and the hit coaxed Spector out of retirement — she released her solo album Unfinished Business in 1987.

title: Take Me Home Tonight

description: The opening track and first single from ELO's 1977 double album Out of the Blue, written and produced by Jeff Lynne. Written in a burst after two weeks of writer's block in a Swiss chalet, it hit No. 13 in the U.S.

pops.text: Track one, single one: 'Turn to Stone' opens the double album Out of the Blue and was its first single, released October 14, 1977.
Written and produced solely by Jeff Lynne — who also played the song's Moog bassline himself.
It very nearly didn't exist: Lynne went to a Swiss chalet to write a double album from scratch and spent the first two weeks in rainy writer's block.
Then the weather cleared — and so did he. The bulk of Out of the Blue, this song included, poured out in the following two-week writing marathon.
Recorded at Musicland Studios in Munich in the summer of 1977, with Lynne taking more control of the sessions than ever before.
That super-fast talking section in the middle? Lynne told Rolling Stone he liked slipping 'something daft' into a song in case it started to drag.
Chart check: No. 13 in the U.S., No. 9 in Canada and No. 18 in the UK, where it spent twelve weeks on the chart.
Odd one out: of Out of the Blue's four singles, this was the only one not to crack the UK top ten.
Flip side trivia: the B-side was 'Mister Kingdom,' a song first released on ELO's 1974 album Eldorado.
Slow-burn vindication: on November 4, 2008, Lynne received a BMI Million-Air certificate for this song — one million radio airplays.

title: Turn to Stone

description: Jeff Lynne's sunshine breakthrough from ELO's 1977 double album Out of the Blue — written the moment Swiss mist lifted, built on orchestra, choir, vocoder and a fire extinguisher, and still cinema's favourite happy song.

pops.text: Writer's block, cured by weather: Jeff Lynne rented a chalet near Lake Geneva to write a double album, got two weeks of mist and nothing, then woke to brilliant sun — and 'Mr. Blue Sky' arrived.
The floodgates opened: Lynne has said he wrote about 14 songs in the two weeks after that sunny morning. Turns out the muse was just waiting for a forecast.
This is the grand finale of 'Concerto for a Rainy Day,' a four-song suite taking up side three of the 1977 double album Out of the Blue — rain first, sunshine last.
It was recorded at Musicland Studios in Munich, the studio Giorgio Moroder built. The album sessions were famously fast for something this layered.
Hear that clanging percussion? Drummer Bev Bevan got it by striking a fire extinguisher — and he would smack one live on stage too.
The robot voice comes from a prototype Vocoder 2000 rushed over from Stuttgart. It arrived with no manual, and the band spent a whole day just coaxing a sound out of it.
Chart check: released as a single in January 1978, it reached No. 6 in the UK but only No. 35 on the Billboard Hot 100. America took a few decades to catch up.
Lynne re-recorded the whole song by himself in 2012 for Mr. Blue Sky: The Very Best of Electric Light Orchestra, playing every instrument at his home studio, Bungalow Palace.
Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 opens with Baby Groot dancing to this while the team fights a monster behind him. Director James Gunn called it joyous, with a dark underpinning.
That final robot voice isn't singing 'Mr. Blue Sky' — Lynne confirmed it says 'Please turn me over.' It was the last track on its vinyl side, so it was literally flipping instructions.

title: Mr. Blue Sky

description: Elton John and Bernie Taupin's 1972 space-age ballad from Honky Château, turning an astronaut into a lonely commuter. A UK No. 2 and US No. 6 hit that became one of Elton's signature songs.

pops.text: Lyricist Bernie Taupin took the idea from Ray Bradbury's 1951 short story 'The Rocket Man,' in The Illustrated Man — a future where being an astronaut is just an everyday job.
Taupin was driving dark back roads to his parents' home in Lincolnshire, stars overhead, when the opening lines arrived whole. He wrote the rest in his head and rushed to get it down at home.
No, it wasn't inspired by David Bowie's 'Space Oddity' — Taupin has denied that for decades. Pure coincidence: both records were produced by Gus Dudgeon.
It was cut in January 1972 at the Château d'Hérouville in France. Taupin typed lyrics upstairs, Elton wrote music at the breakfast-room piano, and songs were often done within the day.
A first for Elton: this is the first song in his catalogue featuring the signature backing-vocal blend of his band — Dee Murray, Nigel Olsson and Davey Johnstone singing together.
That floating synth texture isn't Elton — it's engineer Dave Hentschel on an ARP synthesizer, with Davey Johnstone adding processed slide guitar. Space, courtesy of the control room.
Chart flight path: No. 2 in the UK, where T. Rex's 'Metal Guru' kept it off the top, and No. 6 on the Billboard Hot 100 — Elton's first truly global smash.
In 1978 William Shatner performed it spoken-word at the Saturn Awards, introduced by Taupin himself, complete with three Shatners via video effects. It has been lovingly parodied ever since.
Kate Bush, who called it her favourite song ever, made a reggae-tinged version in 1991 for the tribute album Two Rooms — it was chosen as that album's first single, and she directed its video.
Half a century on, its chorus powered a UK No. 1: Pnau's 2021 mashup 'Cold Heart,' with Dua Lipa, wove 'Rocket Man' together with 'Sacrifice' and two other Elton songs.

title: Rocket Man

description: Bernie Taupin's clear-eyed love letter to a tough 1970s New York, from 1972's Honky Château. Never a hit single, it became one of Elton John's own all-time favourites and his song for the city after 9/11.

pops.text: Bernie Taupin wrote this about his first visit to New York City in 1970 — a trip that included hearing a gun go off near his hotel window. The postcard version of the city didn't survive it.
The opening nods to Ben E. King's 'Spanish Harlem' and its rose in Spanish Harlem. Taupin's reply: now he knows those are not just pretty words — rose trees never grow in New York City.
Like the rest of Honky Château, it was recorded in January 1972 at the Château d'Hérouville in France — a New York song, written by Brits, cut in a French country house.
Productive morning department: Elton has recalled writing the music for this, 'Rocket Man' and 'Amy' in a single day at the château, before the band had even come down to breakfast.
No orchestra, no big band — the record is Elton's piano and voice embellished mainly by just two bandmates: Dee Murray on bass and Davey Johnstone, whose mandolin gives it that flutter.
It was never pushed as a hit single in 1972. Its first single appearance came eight years later, tucked away as the B-side of the UK 'Harmony' single in 1980.
Elton introduced it at his 60th-birthday concert at Madison Square Garden in 2007 as 'one of my all-time favourites' — by then he had performed it more than a hundred times in concert.
On 20 October 2001 Elton sang it at The Concert for New York City at Madison Square Garden, dedicating it to the emergency workers and families still working at the World Trade Center site.
Cameron Crowe put it in Almost Famous, under a New York scene of Penny Lane's loneliness after an overdose of Quaaludes and champagne — the city's glamour and its ache in one track.
Sixteen years later the pair revisited the city in 'Mona Lisas and Mad Hatters (Part Two),' on the 1988 album Reg Strikes Back — same streets, older eyes.

title: Mona Lisas And Mad Hatters

description: Swedish sisters Klara and Johanna Söderberg's 2012 tribute to great harmony duos — Emmylou Harris with Gram Parsons, June Carter with Johnny Cash — from The Lion's Roar, and one of Rolling Stone's best songs of 2012.

pops.text: First Aid Kit are Swedish sisters Klara and Johanna Söderberg. They were just 14 and 16 when they discovered Emmylou Harris and Gram Parsons — and called it a musical revelation.
The chorus is the whole idea in one line: 'I'll be your Emmylou and I'll be your June, and you'll be my Gram and my Johnny too' — Harris and Parsons, June Carter and Johnny Cash.
The sisters call it a tribute to singers who inspired them endlessly: 'When they sing together, it's an otherworldly power. You can hear the love seeping through those vocal cords.'
Their twist on the love song: Johnny and June were married, Emmylou and Gram never officially a couple — 'We may not be able to be together, but at least we can sing together.'
Released 16 January 2012 as the second single from The Lion's Roar, it reached No. 24 on the Swedish singles chart — two Stockholm sisters, charting at home with an American country tribute.
The album was recorded in Omaha, Nebraska, with Bright Eyes producer Mike Mogis, and features Conor Oberst and the Felice Brothers. It went to No. 1 in Sweden.
This video, directed by Maximilla Lukacs, was filmed in Joshua Tree National Park on what would have been Gram Parsons' birthday, with the sisters building a shrine where his coffin was burned.
Rolling Stone named 'Emmylou' the 10th best song of 2012 — and later ranked it No. 96 on its list of the 100 best songs of the 2010s.
Emmylou Harris first heard it by accident, playing in a shop in Adelaide, Australia, while she was on tour. She stopped, thought it beautiful — then heard the voices singing her name.
In 2015 the sisters sang it to Harris herself at Stockholm's Polar Music Prize banquet, where she was a laureate. The performance moved Harris to tears — and they also read her citation.

title: Emmylou

description: First Aid Kit's sweeping 2014 lead single from Stay Gold, all racing strings and sister harmonies about carrying on through change. A European hit that ended up in car ads, video games and TV finales.

pops.text: Released 31 March 2014, this was the first single — and opening track — from Stay Gold, First Aid Kit's third album and their Columbia Records debut.

Klara Söderberg started it sitting in her sister Johanna's apartment: the first verse arrived, she kept singing for a long time, and was wise enough to record it on her phone. Lyrics were picked out of that take.
Both sisters share the songwriting credit, as on most of their work — Klara on guitar and vocals, Johanna on vocals and keyboards, harmonising the way only siblings in the same house can.
It was recorded at ARC Studios in Omaha with producer Mike Mogis, and Stay Gold brought in the Omaha Symphony Orchestra, with arrangements by Nate Walcott. That's the sweep behind the strings.
The sisters drew on Spaghetti Westerns and Lee Hazlewood productions for the album's sound — which explains why this folk song gallops like it's crossing a desert at golden hour.
The video was filmed in an old mansion in Silver Lake, California. The sisters said its theme — things changing, even scaring you, but carrying on anyway — is the song's theme too.
Billboard named it one of the ten best songs of 2014 (so far) in its mid-year list, and Paste later put it at No. 19 on its top 50 songs of the year.
Chart report: No. 7 in Belgium's Flanders chart, No. 19 in France, No. 38 back home in Sweden, and No. 22 on Billboard's US Adult Alternative Songs chart.
Advertisers loved it: in the UK alone it soundtracked TV ads for American Express, Mercedes-Benz and Renault — a silver lining with excellent mileage.

Its afterlife runs long: end credits of the Tales from the Borderlands game finale, a spot in The Umbrella Academy season three, and the ending music of Bad Sisters' final episode. Live, it's often their encore.

title: My Silver Lining

description: A tight instrumental funk workout from Denver six-piece Gold Leader, released as a single in July 2019 on Color Red. It is an early calling card for a band that spent years issuing singles before its debut album.

pops.text: Denver calling! Gold Leader are a six-piece jazz-funk band from Colorado's capital.
No singer, no problem: Gold Leader's music is instrumental, teetering between funk and jazz with a freshly cinematic feel.
Release check: 'Cross Contamination' arrived as a standalone single on July 30, 2019.
Short and punchy for a funk jam: the single clocks in at just 3 minutes 21 seconds.
Early days! This was among the band's first singles — Gold Leader released singles from 2019 onward, nearly a decade before their debut album.
Home label: the track came out on Color Red, the Denver label founded by Eddie Roberts of The New Mastersounds.
This video lives on Color Red's own channel — the label presenting its artist, no bootleg required.
Reviewers hear the Daptone Records revival in the band's DNA, but say Gold Leader sound modern and distinct rather than recreating Motown or Muscle Shoals.
Gold Leader guitarist Thomas Jennings has shared stages, via his various bands, with Lake Street Dive and Snarky Puppy.
The long game paid off: after all those singles, Gold Leader's self-titled debut album finally landed on Color Red with a dozen instrumental tracks.

title: Cross Contamination

description: A slinky instrumental single from Denver jazz-funk outfit Gold Leader, released in November 2020 on Color Red. True to its name, it sneaks along on a tight rhythm section, horns and keys.

pops.text: Sneak attack: 'Creeper' was released as a standalone single on November 6, 2020.
Compact creeper: the track runs just 3 minutes 12 seconds — in, groove, and out.
Genre hop! Apple Music files 'Creeper' under Jazz, while Gold Leader's 2019 single 'Cross Contamination' was filed under Rock.
Denver's own: Gold Leader are billed as a six-piece jazz-funk powerhouse from the Mile High City.
This is the label's official video, posted by Color Red Music — the Denver imprint founded by New Mastersounds guitarist Eddie Roberts.
Instrumental by design: Gold Leader's catalog is built on horns, lush keys, percussive guitar and a highly tight rhythm section.
One year on from their 2019 singles, 'Creeper' kept the band's steady run of one-off releases going toward an eventual debut album.
Praise for the engine room: reviewing the debut album, Spill Magazine singled out drum grooves inspired by J Dilla and Clyde Stubblefield.
Stage-tested sound: Gold Leader rang in a New Year in Denver alongside Neal Francis, delivering what one local review called high-energy, funk-infused music.
Still creeping live: in October 2026 the band headlined a jazz-funk night at Roots Music Project in Boulder, with Thom LaFond opening.

title: Creeper

description: Guns N' Roses' stadium-sized closer from Appetite for Destruction (1987), written in the back of a rental van. Released as a single in January 1989, it peaked at No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100.

pops.text: Born in a van! Slash says the song was written in the back of a rental van, driving home from a San Francisco gig, with the band drinking and playing acoustic guitars.
Lyric vote: Slash offered a much ruder second line for the chorus, preferred it — and was outvoted by the rest of the band. 'Grass is green' won.
Axl explained it in 1988: the verses are about being in the jungle, while the chorus is like being back in the Midwest or somewhere.
Synth spotter: this is the only song on Appetite for Destruction to feature a synthesizer — played by Axl, who is also credited with whistle.
Director Nigel Dick filmed the video at Giants Stadium on August 16, 1988, and at Monsters of Rock at Donington Park four days later.
Look closely at Donington: Nasty Suicide, formerly of Hanoi Rocks — a band Axl often cited as Guns N' Roses' biggest influence — appears in the video.
Single success: released in January 1989, it peaked at No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 6 in the UK, and No. 1 in Ireland.
Stick around: in the last two minutes the song shifts into double time, repeating the chorus while Slash solos over the top.
Closing time: 'Paradise City' has traditionally been the band's show-closing encore song since at least 1988.
Gamers know it: the 2008 game Burnout Paradise is set in a fictional Paradise City named after this song, which plays over its intro and closing credits.

title: Paradise City

description: Guns N' Roses' power ballad, written in 1985 and finally released on Use Your Illusion I in 1991 in its original-lyrics version. It reached No. 10 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 1 in Ireland and Finland.

pops.text: First song alert: Axl Rose has said 'Don't Cry,' written with Izzy Stradlin in March 1985, was the first song written for Guns N' Roses.
Five-minute songwriting! Rose recalled sitting outside the Roxy, being told 'Don't cry' as a goodbye — and writing the song with Stradlin the next night in five minutes.
That high harmony is Shannon Hoon of Blind Melon, singing an octave above Axl. Slash wrote that Hoon's vocal made the song 'all the more soulful.'
Two albums, two versions: the original lyrics sit on Use Your Illusion I, while an alternate-lyrics version is on Use Your Illusion II — only the verse vocals differ.
A third version exists too: a 1986 demo from the Appetite for Destruction sessions, released only on the 'Don't Cry' single.
Story arc: with 'November Rain' and 'Estranged,' this forms a narrative trilogy inspired in part by Del James's short story 'Without You.'
Directors Andy Morahan and Mark Racco shot this multi-million-dollar video, with Hoon joining Axl for the rooftop performance scenes.
Where's Izzy? Co-writer Stradlin skipped the video shoot — a 'Where's Izzy' sign flashes in the clip — and quit the band a month later.
The opening fight over a gun with Stephanie Seymour replays a real incident Rose described from his earlier relationship with Erin Everly.
Chart topper abroad: No. 10 in the US and No. 8 in the UK, but No. 1 in Ireland, Finland and Portugal.

title: Don't Cry

description: The opening track of Herbie Hancock's Fat Albert Rotunda (1969), written for Bill Cosby's Fat Albert TV special. Hancock's first Warner Bros. album turns toward playful jazz-funk and R&B, anchored by his Fender Rhodes.

pops.text: Opening track! 'Wiggle-Waggle' kicks off Fat Albert Rotunda, Herbie Hancock's eighth album, released in December 1969.
Cartoon commission: the music was first written for the NBC special Hey, Hey, Hey, It's Fat Albert, which later inspired Fat Albert and the Cosby Kids.
New label, new sound: this was Hancock's first album for Warner Bros. after leaving Blue Note Records.
Listen to that intro: reviewers note an ominous 20 seconds of sitar-like strumming and echoey trumpet before the single-note guitar line starts the groove.
That busy horn chart is the wiggle: one review calls it as busy and funky as anything James Brown ever did.
Secret weapons: the opening and closing tracks used a bigger, originally uncredited band — Bernard Purdie on drums, Eric Gale and Billy Butler on guitars, and Jerry Jemmott on bass.
Hancock anchors it all on Fender Rhodes electric piano, with fiery solos ahead of him from Joe Henderson and trumpeter Joe Newman on this track.
Recorded at Rudy Van Gelder's studio in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, across sessions in October, November and December 1969.
Single too: 'Wiggle Waggle' was issued as one side of a 1969 Warner Bros. single, backed with 'Fat Mama.'
Prophetic groove: AllMusic calls Fat Albert Rotunda Hancock's first full-fledged venture into jazz-funk — a style he would not revisit until Head Hunters in 1973.

title: Wiggle Waggle
